paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy produces noisy two-dimensional views of biomolecules in many unknown orientations. Reconstructing a molecule requires working out both how each image is oriented and what three-dimensional structure it depicts. When molecules also change conformation, the reconstruction must distinguish those structural changes from differences caused by viewing direction.

cryoFIRE tackles these unknowns together. An encoder estimates each image’s pose and conformation, while a decoder based on imaging physics combines the observations into an implicit neural representation of conformational variation. The approach is amortized: a shared inference model estimates these quantities across the dataset, avoiding an expensive pose-search step for individual images. It supports reconstruction from scratch with unknown poses.

The authors report that this approach can deliver an order-of-magnitude speedup on datasets containing millions of images without losing accuracy. They also demonstrate that jointly estimating pose and conformation can be amortized across the dataset, and that the resulting method extracts interpretable information about molecular dynamics from experimental data. The contribution therefore connects computational efficiency with recovering meaningful structural variation.
neurips-2022-amortized-inference-for-het.tldr: cryoFIRE jointly estimates molecular poses and conformations with shared neural inference, enabling faster heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction.

paragraphs: Avalon is a benchmark for testing whether reinforcement learning agents can use learned skills in unfamiliar situations. Agents inhabit procedurally generated three-dimensional worlds, where survival involves finding food, navigating terrain, and avoiding hazards. Its 20 tasks span relatively simple actions, such as eating and throwing, through more involved activities such as hunting and navigation.

The benchmark holds the reward function, world dynamics, and available actions constant across tasks. Different tasks arise entirely from changes to the environment. This shared structure lets researchers study generalization to new worlds within a task, transfer between tasks, and combinations that require previously learned skills to work together. The environment becomes the controlled source of variation.

Avalon includes an efficient simulator, baseline implementations, and scoring metrics evaluated against hundreds of hours of human performance. These resources are publicly available and open source. Standard reinforcement learning baselines improve on most tasks, but remain well below human performance. Those results suggest the benchmark provides substantial room to investigate generalization, including whether agents can compose skills beyond the situations used for training.
neurips-2022-avalon-a-benchmark-for-rl-g.tldr: Avalon tests reinforcement learning generalization through diverse survival tasks that share actions, dynamics, and rewards.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses promising evaluations of an expensive function using a probabilistic model and an acquisition function. Selecting the next evaluation becomes difficult when design choices include discrete variables: ordinary gradients cannot directly move between categories, while checking every possible combination can be prohibitively expensive.

The paper replaces direct acquisition-function optimization with optimization over a distribution of candidate designs. Continuous parameters control that distribution, and the objective is the expected acquisition value. Under suitable reparameterizations, maximizing this probabilistic objective selects the same policy as maximizing the original acquisition function. Consequently, the corresponding policy retains the original regret bounds.

The authors provide scalable, unbiased estimators of the new objective and its gradient, and prove convergence to a stationary point under gradient ascent. Recovering an acquisition-function maximizer is a further result tied to increasing both the number of starting points and gradient steps; stationary convergence alone is not the same claim. Experiments report state-of-the-art optimization performance across real applications. The approach also complements other advances and extends naturally to multiple objectives and unknown constraints.
neurips-2022-bayesian-optimization-over-.tldr: Probabilistic reparameterization makes discrete Bayesian optimization amenable to gradient methods while preserving the original policy under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: A predictive model can perform well on familiar data by exploiting correlations that stop being useful in a new environment. This shortcut learning creates a gap between accuracy on the training distribution and reliability under distribution shifts. Addressing the problem requires identifying which available signals act as shortcuts.

The paper proposes a two-stage approach: first identify relevant shortcuts efficiently, then use that information to train predictors that are more robust to shifts. Its key requirement is access during training to auxiliary labels, potentially a large collection, some of which describe possible shortcuts. This provides a pool from which to identify relevant shortcuts without assuming their precise set is already known or recoverable from saliency maps.

The authors give theoretical and empirical evidence that their approach can identify a sufficient set of shortcuts and produce more efficient predictors with finite samples. Sufficiency matters here: the stated result does not require identifying every conceivable shortcut. The contribution links shortcut discovery to predictor construction, while making the availability of auxiliary training labels a substantive part of the method’s setting.
neurips-2022-causally-motivated-multi-sh.tldr: The method uses auxiliary training labels to identify a sufficient set of shortcuts and build more robust predictors.

paragraphs: Continual graph learning asks models to learn new tasks from newly arriving graph data while retaining performance on earlier tasks. Comparing methods is difficult because graph datasets have varied structures, and existing studies configure tasks and evaluations differently. An apparent difference between methods can therefore be entangled with differences in experimental setup.

CGLB organizes this area into a common benchmark assembled from public datasets. It includes tasks that make predictions about individual nodes and tasks that make predictions about whole graphs. Both are considered under task-incremental and class-incremental settings. The authors describe class-incremental learning as more practical and challenging, while also being less explored in existing work.

The accompanying toolkit supports training, evaluation, and visualization, reducing the repeated work needed to prepare experiments. The paper also explains how its task configurations differ from one another and relate to classical continual learning settings, then compares leading baselines within this framework. Its central contribution is a shared experimental foundation that makes method comparisons easier to interpret and lets researchers spend more effort on models.
neurips-2022-cglb-benchmark-tasks-for-co.tldr: CGLB standardizes continual graph learning tasks and provides tools for comparing methods across multiple experimental settings.

paragraphs: Coordinate-based neural representations describe a scene continuously through a network that takes spatial coordinates as input. They support surface reconstruction and rendering new viewpoints, but approaches such as NeRF commonly need many calibrated images to achieve good results. CoCo-INR addresses this dependence by enriching coordinate features with prior information about geometry and appearance.

The method uses two attention modules with different jobs. Codebook attention selects useful prototypes from a prior codebook, drawing on the geometric and visual information they contain. Coordinate attention then distributes this information to individual coordinates. This gives the representation additional information for describing a particular scene or object surface when fewer input views are available.

Experiments cover scene reconstruction on DTU and BlendedMVS as well as full head reconstruction on H3DS. The authors report more photorealistic appearance and geometry than current comparison methods with fewer calibrated images, together with robustness to reduced view counts and preservation of fine detail. The findings support using prior information to strengthen coordinate-based reconstruction when observations are relatively sparse.
neurips-2022-coordinates-are-not-lonely-.tldr: CoCo-INR injects codebook information into coordinate features to improve 3D reconstruction from fewer calibrated views.

paragraphs: Differential privacy adds randomness to released data, which complicates statistical inference about the confidential data that generated it. Computing the likelihood of a private release can require integrating over a huge space of possible confidential databases. For Bayesian analysis, the resulting posterior is doubly intractable, making traditional MCMC techniques inapplicable in the setting described.

The proposed framework introduces the unobserved confidential data as additional variables alongside the model parameters. Its sampling algorithm alternates between updating these two groups. This turns the hidden database into part of the inference procedure. For the difficult confidential-data update, the authors develop a generic approach that uses the privacy mechanism’s guarantee to support efficient sampling.

The paper provides results on computational complexity, acceptance rates, and mixing, addressing both the cost of sampling and how the chain explores its target distribution. Demonstrations use a naïve-Bayes log-linear model and linear regression. The framework is intended to cover a broad range of statistical models and privacy mechanisms, providing a route to Bayesian inference that explicitly accounts for the privatization process.
neurips-2022-data-augmentation-mcmc-for-.tldr: The framework alternates between hidden confidential data and model parameters to make Bayesian inference from privatized releases tractable.

paragraphs: Decision-based black-box attacks test a model through its returned decisions, making query efficiency central to finding small adversarial perturbations. The paper argues that existing attacks lose efficiency by overlooking differences in noise sensitivity across image regions. This is particularly relevant to vision transformers, whose interactions between patches reduce sensitivity to local noise.

Patch-wise Adversarial Removal, or PAR, treats regions separately. A coarse-to-fine search divides an image into patches, and the method tracks both the noise magnitude and noise sensitivity of each patch. It then chooses the patch with the highest query value for further noise compression. This directs queries toward local reductions according to the information collected about each region.

The authors support the approach with a theoretical analysis of existing attacks’ limitations and experiments on three datasets. PAR achieves substantially smaller perturbations for the same query count in those experiments. It can also initialize other decision-based attacks, improving noise compression on both transformers and convolutional networks without additional calculations as reported. The findings show why region-aware search matters when assessing robustness with limited queries.
neurips-2022-decision-based-black-box-at.tldr: PAR uses patch-specific noise sensitivity to find smaller adversarial perturbations with the same number of model queries.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can achieve strong accuracy, yet their architecture and operators often make them slower than lightweight convolutional networks. This creates a deployment problem for real-time applications on mobile devices. EfficientFormer investigates whether transformer design can retain high accuracy while reaching the latency of MobileNet.

The authors first examine transformer architectures and operators to identify inefficient choices. They then introduce a dimension-consistent transformer design that does not incorporate MobileNet blocks. A latency-driven slimming procedure produces a family of models. Actual inference latency therefore guides the final architecture choices, connecting the design process directly to the deployment goal.

On an iPhone 12 using CoreML, EfficientFormer-L1 reaches 79.2% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 1.6 milliseconds of inference latency. The stated MobileNetV2 comparison has the same latency and 74.7% accuracy. The larger EfficientFormer-L7 reaches 83.3% accuracy at 7.0 milliseconds. These results demonstrate that carefully designed transformers can combine strong accuracy with low mobile latency under the reported hardware and compilation setup, while offering multiple points along the accuracy–speed tradeoff.
neurips-2022-efficientformer-vision-tran.tldr: EfficientFormer combines transformer architecture changes and latency-driven slimming to achieve strong accuracy at mobile inference speeds.

paragraphs: Equilibrium propagation offers a way to train neural networks using local learning rules, making it relevant to neuromorphic systems and models of biological learning. However, its requirement for infinitesimal teaching signals is problematic in noisy physical systems. Separate temporal phases and limited application at scale present additional obstacles.

The paper extends equilibrium propagation to holomorphic networks. Within this framework, the authors analytically derive exact gradients using teaching signals with finite amplitude. The gradient can be obtained from the first Fourier coefficient of continuous neuronal activity oscillations. This provides a way to extract the learning signal from oscillatory activity without requiring separate phases.

Numerical simulations show robust gradient estimation in the presence of noise and benefits from finite teaching signals in deeper models. The authors also establish an equilibrium-propagation benchmark on ImageNet at 32-by-32 resolution, matching an equivalent network trained with backpropagation. The work combines an analytical gradient result with computational evidence, offering a formal account of how oscillations could support learning in biological or neuromorphic systems.
neurips-2022-holomorphic-equilibrium-pro.tldr: Holomorphic equilibrium propagation derives exact gradients from finite oscillations and supports learning without separate temporal phases.

paragraphs: Query-based instance segmentation models use learned embeddings to find individual objects in image features and produce their masks. Their success depends on queries distinguishing one instance from another. This paper introduces a training framework that strengthens that relationship through two properties: uniqueness across the dataset and consistent behavior under geometric transformations.

For uniqueness, queries must retrieve their corresponding instances across the entire training dataset rather than only within a single scene. The harder retrieval task pressures embeddings to distinguish instances more effectively. For transformation equivariance, training encourages both image representations and queries to change consistently with geometric transformations, supporting more reliable matching between them.

The framework improves four existing segmentation models: CondInst, SOLOv2, SOTR, and Mask2Former. Reported gains on COCO range from 1.6 to 3.2 average-precision points, and SOLOv2 improves by 2.7 points on LVISv1. These results support the value of improving how queries are learned across multiple architectures. The contribution is a training strategy that makes instance identity and geometric consistency explicit objectives for query-based segmentation.
neurips-2022-learning-equivariant-segmen.tldr: Training queries for dataset-wide instance distinction and geometric equivariance improves several query-based segmentation models.

paragraphs: Molecular prediction models are often developed and evaluated with training and test data drawn from the same distribution. In applications, molecules may instead come from unfamiliar environments, including different scaffold or size distributions. MoleOOD addresses the resulting loss of reliability by seeking molecular features whose relationship with the prediction target remains more stable.

The framework is motivated by the observation that molecular properties are often associated with particular substructures across environments. An environment-inference model learns latent factors affecting how data arise from different distributions. A separate learning objective guides the molecule encoder toward substructures that relate consistently to labels across those inferred environments. Environment specifications do not have to be supplied manually.

Experiments on ten real-world datasets show stronger generalization than existing methods across several out-of-distribution settings. The authors report improvements of up to 5.9% on OGB and 3.9% on DrugOOD over the strongest baselines, measured by ROC-AUC. These are reported maximum gains, not uniform improvements across every dataset. The results support learning stable substructure–label relationships while inferring environmental variation from data.
neurips-2022-learning-substructure-invar.tldr: MoleOOD learns latent environments and stable molecular substructures to improve prediction under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning improves an agent by updating its action-selection policy. Constrained methods regulate these updates by keeping the new policy near a previous one. The paper examines how to choose this reference more flexibly, particularly when the immediately preceding policy performs poorly and may be an unhelpful guide for the next update.

Memory-Constrained Policy Optimization, or MCPO, uses two trust regions. One constrains proximity to the single old policy, as in earlier approaches. The other uses a virtual policy that represents a broader range of past policies. A mechanism constructs this virtual policy automatically from a memory buffer, allowing the method to select appropriate trust regions dynamically during optimization.

The authors evaluate MCPO on robotic locomotion, navigation with sparse rewards, and Atari games. Across these environments, it consistently delivers competitive performance against recent on-policy constrained policy-gradient methods. The stated result supports using policy history to regulate learning across different tasks. Its distinctive contribution is making past policies an active part of update constraints, with potential benefit when the most recent policy performs poorly.
neurips-2022-learning-to-constrain-polic.tldr: MCPO constrains policy updates using both the previous policy and an automatically constructed reference drawn from policy history.

paragraphs: Updating only a small fraction of a pretrained model’s parameters does not necessarily produce equally large training-memory savings. If those parameters sit inside the backbone, computing their gradients can still require backpropagation through the large model. Ladder Side-Tuning addresses this distinction between the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed to train them.

LST trains a small, separate network that receives intermediate backbone activations through shortcut connections called ladders. This side network makes the predictions. Backpropagation runs through the side network and ladder connections, avoiding the need to backpropagate through the backbone. The architecture therefore changes the gradient-computation path as well as reducing the trainable parameter count.

Across language and vision-and-language evaluations, LST reports 69% memory savings relative to full fine-tuning, compared with 26% for other methods using similar parameter counts. It outperforms Adapter and LoRA in a low-memory regime. Experiments with larger T5 models also achieve better GLUE performance than full fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient methods. Vision-and-language results show similar accuracy to alternatives with substantially greater memory savings.
neurips-2022-lst-ladder-side-tuning-for-.tldr: Ladder Side-Tuning reduces adaptation memory by training a small side network without backpropagating through the pretrained backbone.

paragraphs: Single-step adversarial training is computationally attractive, but it can undergo catastrophic overfitting: a model suddenly becomes vulnerable to attacks that use multiple steps. Adding a random perturbation before the single-step attack can help, yet earlier work found that this approach still fails at larger perturbation sizes. A proposed regularizer addressed the failure at substantial computational cost.

This paper revisits two choices in the training procedure: how much noise to add around a clean sample and whether to clip it. The authors find that stronger noise combined with omitting clipping is highly effective at avoiding catastrophic overfitting for large perturbation radii. They build this finding into Noise-FGSM, or N-FGSM.

Across a broad experimental suite, N-FGSM avoids the reported failure while retaining the efficiency benefits of single-step training. It matches or exceeds the performance of GradAlign and runs three times faster in the reported comparisons. The findings show that the noise and clipping choices can materially change training stability, offering an empirically supported way to obtain robust training without the cost of that regularizer.
neurips-2022-make-some-noise-reliable-an.tldr: Noise-FGSM combines stronger noise with no clipping to avoid catastrophic overfitting in experiments while accelerating adversarial training.

paragraphs: Collaborative inference divides a deep-learning model between a local device and a cloud system to speed prediction. This arrangement can expose private inputs because a malicious cloud provider may reconstruct them from the representations it receives. Existing defenses attempt to protect those representations, but their resistance to reconstruction needs to be tested.

The paper studies the robustness of such defenses and observes that sensitive information can remain in representations even after they have been obfuscated. Motivated by this finding, the authors develop Sensitive Feature Distillation, or SFD, to recover sensitive information from protected features. The method serves as a way to probe what the defenses actually conceal.

Experiments show that SFD penetrates the examined defenses in model-partitioning scenarios. These results demonstrate inadequacies in the tested mechanisms as protection against reconstruction attacks. The practical implication is that altering or obscuring a representation can leave recoverable private information inside it. By exposing this residual information, the work provides evidence for improving how collaborative-inference defenses are designed and assessed.
neurips-2022-measuring-data-reconstructi.tldr: Sensitive Feature Distillation recovers private information from protected intermediate representations, exposing weaknesses in evaluated collaborative-inference defenses.

paragraphs: NeuPhysics learns the three-dimensional geometry and physical parameters of a dynamic scene from a single RGB video stream. Its representation separates a stable description of shape from changes over time. A time-invariant signed distance function provides the reference geometry, while a time-conditioned deformation field describes motion relative to that reference.

The method connects this neural representation to a differentiable physics simulator through a two-way conversion involving a hexahedral mesh. This connection allows the system to estimate physical parameters from the source video by minimizing a cycle-consistency loss. The neural field and mesh serve complementary roles within the same reconstruction process, linking visual geometry with simulated physical behavior.

The mesh also provides an editing interface: users modify recovered three-dimensional objects, and those changes propagate back into the neural field. Experiments report better mesh and video reconstruction of dynamic scenes than competing neural-field approaches. Examples using consumer-camera videos demonstrate useful recovered representations. The contribution therefore combines reconstruction, physics estimation, and interactive editing within a method that takes monocular video as its input.
neurips-2022-neuphysics-editable-neural-.tldr: NeuPhysics connects neural geometry with a physics simulator to reconstruct and edit dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video.

paragraphs: Generic neural networks for motor control must learn useful behavior with little architectural guidance. The paper asks whether structure inspired by biological motor circuits can make learning more efficient and behavior easier to interpret. Its starting point is the highly organized circuitry that helps animals act effectively early in life.

The authors translate locomotion circuits from C. elegans into a neural network controlling a simulated Swimmer agent. On the locomotion task, the network begins with good performance and eventually reaches performance comparable to multilayer perceptrons. It learns much more efficiently from experience and uses orders of magnitude fewer parameters. The architecture is also interpretable and transfers to new body designs.

Ablation experiments distinguish the roles of different design choices. Constraints on excitation and inhibition are crucial for learning, while weight initialization contributes to strong initial behavior. These results suggest that biological inspiration can supply useful architectural biases for motor control, with different ingredients helping at different stages. The evidence comes from the studied locomotion setting and motivates investigation of more complex embodied control.
neurips-2022-neural-circuit-architectura.tldr: A network inspired by worm locomotion circuitry learns simulated swimming efficiently with far fewer parameters than generic networks.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning agents can struggle when their surroundings look different from the training environment. Existing approaches often vary the appearance of observations already available within that environment. This paper investigates a broader source of visual experience: representations learned beforehand from a large collection of real-world images.

The authors find that early layers of an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet provide representations that generalize well for visual reinforcement learning. They use this finding to build PIE-G, a framework designed to transfer to unseen visual scenarios in a zero-shot manner. The central idea is to reuse suitable off-the-shelf visual features as part of the agent’s representation.

Evaluations cover the DMControl Generalization Benchmark, DMControl Manipulation Tasks, Drawer World, and CARLA. The empirical results suggest improved sample efficiency and substantially better generalization than previous leading methods. In the challenging video-background setting, the authors report an average generalization-performance gain of 55%. These findings support the usefulness of early pretrained visual features for the tested control settings and show that image pretraining can benefit policies facing unfamiliar appearances.
neurips-2022-pre-trained-image-encoder-f.tldr: PIE-G reuses early ImageNet-pretrained ResNet features to improve visual reinforcement learning generalization to unseen appearances.

paragraphs: Training commonly uses stochastic gradient descent for multiple passes over a dataset, but much generalization theory concerns a single pass. Other analyses describe worst-case problems, which can obscure behavior on a particular dataset. This paper studies multi-pass SGD for least squares in the interpolation regime and seeks a bound sensitive to the individual problem.

The resulting excess-risk bound depends on iteration count, step size, and data covariance. The authors also derive an exact decomposition: SGD’s excess risk equals gradient descent’s excess risk plus a positive fluctuation term. Within this analyzed setting, the decomposition indicates that SGD generalizes worse than gradient descent on an instance-by-instance basis under the comparison.

Computational cost changes the practical interpretation. SGD requires more iterations to reach the same excess-risk level, yet uses fewer stochastic gradient evaluations overall. The authors therefore find it preferable in computational time within their analysis. The work separates progress per iteration from the work needed to reach a target error, explaining how worse statistical progress per update can coexist with better computational efficiency.
neurips-2022-risk-bounds-of-multi-pass-s.tldr: For interpolating least squares, instance-dependent bounds show SGD’s additional risk relative to gradient descent alongside its computational advantage.

paragraphs: Representing a video with a coordinate-based neural network requires balancing training cost, reconstruction quality, and parameter count. Improving one can make another less attractive. Neural Video Representations with Learnable Positional Features, or NVP, addresses these objectives together by storing shared video content in learned latent features.

The architecture uses two-dimensional latent keyframes designed to capture common content across spatial and temporal axes. These learnable positional features encode information that the coordinate-based representation can reuse. The authors also compress the latent codes with existing image and video codecs, connecting the neural representation to established compression tools for computational and memory efficiency.

On the UVG benchmark, NVP trains twice as fast as prior approaches, taking less than five minutes, while using more than eight times fewer parameters. Reported reconstruction quality rises from 34.07 to 34.57 in PSNR. The paper also demonstrates video inpainting and frame interpolation. Together, the findings show that learned latent positional information can improve the reported quality, training-speed, and parameter-efficiency tradeoff while supporting additional video operations.
neurips-2022-scalable-neural-video-repre.tldr: NVP uses learned latent keyframes to improve neural video encoding quality while reducing training time and parameter count.

paragraphs: Structural pruning simplifies a network by removing components, with the goal of making inference faster while preserving accuracy. Hardware-Aware Latency Pruning, or HALP, frames this as a global allocation problem: choose a pruned architecture that maximizes accuracy while meeting a specified latency budget on the target device.

HALP combines two signals when ranking filters. A latency lookup table estimates potential speed gains, and a global saliency score estimates the accuracy consequences of removal. Both are inexpensive to evaluate during pruning. An augmented knapsack solver then uses this information to make coordinated choices across the network under the latency constraint.

Experiments span classification and detection, multiple networks, and different platforms. On ImageNet, pruned ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 improve throughput by 1.60 and 1.90 times, with top-1 accuracy changes of +0.3% and −0.2%, respectively. For SSD on VOC, throughput improves 1.94 times with a 0.56 mAP decrease. The authors report consistently stronger tradeoffs than prior methods. These results support treating device latency and accuracy impact jointly when allocating a network’s remaining structure.
neurips-2022-structural-pruning-via-late.tldr: HALP uses a knapsack formulation to prune networks globally according to accuracy impact and target-device latency.

paragraphs: Dollar Street addresses a representation problem in computer vision: datasets need images from varied populations and accurate demographic information to support robust and fair models. The dataset contains 38,479 photographs of everyday household items from homes around the world, making geographic and socioeconomic variation part of the data itself.

The images are manually curated and fully labeled with object categories such as toilets, toothbrushes, and stoves. They also carry demographic information including region, country, and monthly household income. Collection includes homes without internet access and households earning as little as $26.99 per month, bringing in visual examples from populations traditionally underrepresented in image datasets.

The authors show that using Dollar Street can improve classification performance for household-item images from lower-income homes. This is a concrete demonstrated benefit of broader representation, rather than a claim that the dataset resolves every source of bias. All images and associated data use a CC-BY license, allowing academic and commercial use. The contribution combines labeled visual diversity with demographic context that helps make differences between populations visible.
neurips-2022-the-dollar-street-dataset-i.tldr: Dollar Street provides globally diverse household images and demographic labels, improving reported classification performance for lower-income homes.

paragraphs: The paper distinguishes two intervention problems in causal discovery: verifying a proposed causal graph and searching for the correct graph. Both aim to minimize interventions, but verification begins with a candidate answer. The authors use the minimum cost of verification as a reference for understanding the harder search problem.

For verification, they characterize a smallest set of atomic interventions that is necessary and sufficient to check a claimed graph. The characterization uses covered edges and extends to interventions of bounded size and costs that depend on the targeted node. They provide efficient algorithms with provable optimality or near-optimality guarantees for computing verifying sets on general graphs.

For search, an adaptive algorithm based on graph separators fully orients an essential graph using O(log n) times the underlying graph’s optimal atomic verifying size. A worst-case lower bound for essential line graphs shows this logarithmic comparison is tight. When interventions can affect at most k nodes, the approximation becomes O(log n · log k). These guarantees quantify search effort relative to verification, rather than treating the two tasks as interchangeable.
neurips-2022-verification-and-search-alg.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient causal-graph verification and bounds adaptive search costs relative to optimal verification.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search represents candidate operations with trainable architecture parameters and estimates their gradients through approximations. The authors find empirically that these approximations can distort the loss landscape, biasing the objective and producing inaccurate gradients. ZARTS explores zero-order optimization as a way to search without imposing those approximations.

The paper evaluates three zero-order methods, named RS, MGS, and GLD. MGS provides the best balance of accuracy and speed among them. The authors also examine connections between RS, MGS, and gradient descent, interpreting ZARTS as a robust gradient-free counterpart to DARTS. The contribution changes how architecture choices are optimized within the search process.

Experiments cover multiple datasets and search spaces, including 12 benchmarks where DARTS suffers performance collapse from instability. ZARTS shows strong robustness in these comparisons. In the DARTS search space, its discovered architecture reaches 97.54% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 75.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. Combining ZARTS with three complementary DARTS variants further improves speed and performance, suggesting the optimization change can work alongside other search improvements.
neurips-2022-zarts-on-zero-order-optimiz.tldr: ZARTS uses zero-order architecture optimization to avoid problematic DARTS approximations and improve empirical search robustness.
